overview: This record follows Portuguese coastal settlements and the later colony in what became Guinea-Bissau. Early merchants operated among powerful African communities; a European fort did not mean control of the surrounding country. Cacheu connected river commerce to Atlantic slave trading. Portuguese Guinea became administratively separate from Cape Verde in 1879.

periods.title: Ports among African societies
periods.summary: Coastal commerce depended on local networks and authority.

periods.title: A separate colonial administration
periods.summary: Bolama became the capital of the separately administered colony.

items.text: The imported map needs caution: its early outline marks coastal pockets, but the 1878 to 1914 snapshots shift north into Casamance and toward Gambia. They are not a reliable picture of Portuguese control. The 1914 outline returns to Guinea-Bissau; 1920 is this label’s endpoint, not independence.

Cacheu’s surviving riverside fort is dated to 1641 to 1647 by the heritage inventory. Its plan is only about 20 metres square, with small corner bastions and walls roughly four to five metres high. A compact fort could guard a trading post without governing an entire region.

Crispina Peres ran a major seventeenth-century trading household in Cacheu. When her husband was incapacitated by gout, she managed its business with sailors, servants and enslaved workers. Her commercial power was real, and so was the exploitation of people within that economy.

Seventeenth-century Cacheu had two contrasting neighborhoods. Villa Fria contained the fort, officials and merchants; a palisade separated it from Villa Quente, where African trading families connected the port to regional commercial networks.

An earlier letter from Cacheu, dated 30 May 1641, reports agreements with neighboring African rulers and nobles. The archival catalogue also lists wax, ivory and enslaved people in its trade discussion. Diplomacy with surrounding communities was a practical necessity for the small Portuguese establishment.

Rice farming was already sophisticated before this map record begins. A sixteenth-century account describes farmers building earth barriers around floodplain fields to hold back river water. The barriers sometimes broke. Keeping dinner growing meant understanding water levels and repairing defenses, not merely scattering seeds.

An early description of the Cacheu region records Diola farmers using small canoes to cross flooded rice fields. Imagine commuting to the crops by boat. Water could nourish a harvest and obstruct the farmer, making transport part of the agricultural skill set.

Historian Lourenço Ocuni Cá describes community education through participation: children joined fieldwork, listened to elders’ stories and watched communal ceremonies. They learned practical skills and social responsibilities together. Much learning took place in the family and community, beyond the institutions counted in colonial school reports.

Peres’s trial also reveals family responses to sickness: she sought local healers and a herbal pouch for her ill daughter. The Inquisition turned such practices into accusations. These records tell us about care and persecution; they do not establish that the remedies worked.

In 1914 Bolama’s administration asked for proposals to electrify the town, but received no response. It was also struggling with water infrastructure. The historian found no stated explanation for the failed tender. An ambitious announcement and a working service were very different things.

Bolama’s town hall was commissioned in 1919. The 43-metre building has ten Tuscan columns supporting a triangular pediment, a front staircase and a long sheltered balcony behind. Its imposing public face offers a striking contrast to the difficulties of supplying everyday services.

A writing sample from an 1843 Portuguese publication is “Memoria sobre o estado actual de Senegambia portugueza”: “Report on the present state of Portuguese Senegambia.” This catalogue-transcribed title preserves older spelling. It represents the Portuguese language of colonial print, alongside the region’s many African languages and oral traditions.

The colony continued long after this map label stops. Portugal’s formal recognition of Guinea-Bissau’s independence was signed on 10 September 1974 and published the next day. That document names a sovereign republic; it does not describe the disappearance of the region’s people or cultures.

ending.text: The 1920 map cutoff was not the end of Portuguese rule. The colonial administration eventually gave way to independent Guinea-Bissau; Portugal formally recognized the republic on 10 September 1974.
